A reinvested fund distribution can still need tax cash: plan the provision before buying more units

Four editable charts separate reinvestment, retained cash, an assumed distribution-tax liability and an unfunded provision in a non-registered fund account.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 7 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

The central idea

Reinvestment changes where value is held; it does not automatically remove distribution tax. Identify the applicable tax treatment and cash funding before treating every distributed dollar as available for more units.

01

Reinvestment and tax funding answer different questions

A fund can reinvest a distribution automatically, leaving the investor with more units and little new bank cash. That can support continued investment, but it does not establish that the distribution carries no tax consequence.

CRA’s mutual-fund guidance explains that distributions in a non-registered holding can have different income characters, that reinvested amounts may still need reporting, and that sales and cost-base records create separate calculations. This article takes the cash-funding question as its focus. It does not determine the character of an actual distribution or complete a tax return.

The tool uses a hypothetical provision factor applied to the gross distribution. Its 30% default means “set aside thirty cents per distributed dollar in this example.” It is not a statement that a particular investor’s Canadian marginal rate, withholding rate or capital-gains inclusion rate is 30%.

A liability and its funding are separate records. The fund may be valuable enough to sell something later, but that is not the same as having dedicated cash ready. The charts identify any gap without silently borrowing, adding outside income or assuming an additional sale has no tax cost.

02

Reconcile the distribution before calling it extra profit

The example begins immediately before a distribution with 500 units at a net asset value, or NAV, of CAD 21. Fund value is CAD 10,500. A CAD 1 distribution per original unit totals CAD 500.

Assuming no other price movement, the distribution reduces NAV to CAD 20. The original units are then worth CAD 10,000, with CAD 500 distributed separately. Those two values still add to CAD 10,500. The distribution has moved existing value; it has not created another CAD 500 on top of the original statement.

If all CAD 500 is reinvested at CAD 20, it purchases 25 new units. The resulting 525 units are worth CAD 10,500. If none is reinvested, the investor instead holds CAD 10,000 of fund units and CAD 500 cash. The first chart compares these allocations using the same original resources.

The example assumes an ordinary event where cash can be retained or reinvested. Some non-cash distributions do not provide that choice. Actual ex-distribution and payment dates, price changes and issuer terms require their own records; the immediate event here abstracts from them.

03

Read the full-reinvestment cash gap directly

Apply the hypothetical 30% provision to CAD 500. The modeled liability is CAD 150. With full reinvestment and no dedicated outside cash, the fund remains worth CAD 10,500 but cash available for that provision is zero. The funding gap is therefore CAD 150.

It would be misleading to show the larger unit count as a complete financial gain while ignoring the liability. The waterfall starts with pre-distribution fund value, adds only separately entered outside cash, and deducts the provision once. With the defaults, resources net of this modeled liability are CAD 10,350.

That economic net figure does not mean the provision has been paid. A household with CAD 10,500 inside the fund and a CAD 150 unfunded liability has a cash-management decision to make, even though its net amount can be calculated.

The tool does not sell units to solve the gap. A real sale could introduce a capital gain or loss, transaction costs, settlement timing and additional cash effects. Those cannot be assumed away merely because the initial gap looks small.

04

Retaining some distribution cash can fund the same provision

With no outside cash, retaining CAD 150 and reinvesting CAD 350 funds the default provision. Reinvestment buys 17.5 units at CAD 20. The fund then holds 517.5 units worth CAD 10,350, alongside CAD 150 earmarked cash.

Before deducting the liability, total resources remain CAD 10,500. After deducting it, net resources remain CAD 10,350. Compared with full reinvestment, the immediate economic net amount is unchanged; the location of value and availability of cash differ.

The maximum reinvestment funded without a sale or new outside money is 70% of the distribution in this example. This is a cash constraint derived from the assumed provision, not a recommended reinvestment percentage or an optimal investment allocation.

If all CAD 500 is retained instead, the provision leaves CAD 350 cash and CAD 10,000 invested. Future outcomes can differ because a different amount remains exposed to market returns. The immediate equality shown here should not be extended into a claim that every reinvestment policy produces the same long-term result.

05

Count dedicated outside cash once and name its purpose

Now enter CAD 150 of dedicated outside cash that already exists before the distribution. Full reinvestment can then coexist with a funded CAD 150 provision. But the scenario began with CAD 150 more total resources than the zero-outside-cash example.

It is not a free improvement in the fund’s tax treatment. The separately entered cash is part of the household balance sheet and is counted in every allocation bar. Using it for this provision means it cannot simultaneously remain available for another bill or be counted as an untouched emergency reserve.

The line chart subtracts the full provision from available cash at each possible reinvestment percentage. A negative result identifies a gap; zero means the entered cash just covers the provision; a positive result leaves cash after that earmark. The zero crossing is the cash constraint, rather than a forecast of a tax authority’s assessment.

The matrix changes both the reinvestment percentage and provision factor. It shows how sensitive cash needs are to the assumed tax amount. The selected factor drives the main example, while the matrix’s fixed alternatives are teaching scenarios rather than a table of applicable rates.

06

Evaluate tax efficiency without confusing the fund with its account

A balanced mutual fund, equity fund or other pooled investment can distribute different types of amounts. The actual tax result depends on the holding, account, income character and investor circumstances. Choosing automatic reinvestment does not itself answer those questions.

This tool is restricted to a non-registered illustration. TFSA and RRSP rules are separate account rules; do not copy its provision into a registered plan as though the same distribution event necessarily produces a current personal tax bill. The balanced-fund account discussion and matched-effort RRSP/TFSA charts explain that distinction with CRA sources.

Keep cost records separate as well. More units can affect the average cost calculation, and return of capital has different cost-base consequences. The fund cost-base guide models those records. This cash tool calculates neither adjusted cost base nor a capital gain.

Efficient investing connects the underlying exposure, costs, account and cash plan. A large distribution yield is not proof of a high total return, and keeping all distributed dollars invested is not automatically the most workable choice for someone who must fund tax elsewhere.

07

Use an estimate as a provision, then reconcile it with the actual record

Before a distribution, identify whether the holding allows cash retention or reinvestment, what information is available about its expected character, and what other cash is genuinely earmarked. An estimate can help prepare the budget, provided it remains labelled as an estimate.

After the event, reconcile the issuer’s statement, unit count and tax slips with the relevant account records. If the actual tax effect differs from the provision, update both the liability estimate and its funding. Do not keep using a convenient percentage simply because it made the earlier chart balance.

Payment dates also matter. This tool puts the provision beside the distribution to expose the funding requirement; it does not establish a filing deadline, instalment obligation or the date a particular tax payment is due. Those belong in a separate verified calendar.

The practical sequence is to understand the event, estimate its applicable liability, identify the cash, and then decide how much to reinvest. That preserves the distinction between growing an investment position and having the money available to meet the obligations connected with it.
